samples.text:
Today in many countries, doctors are using artificial intelligence to find out what illness a patient have. I believe that this technology has more advantages than disadvantages, but we should be careful how we use it.

The main advantage is that AI can be very accurate. A computer program can look at thousands of X-rays and scans and it can learn to notice small problems which a human doctor might miss. For example, it can find early signs of cancer, and this can save many lifes. Another benefit is speed. Doctors in busy hospitals do not have enough time for every patient, but AI can check the results in a few seconds, so patients get their diagnosis more faster. This is also useful in poor areas where there is not many doctors.

However, there are some disadvantages. First, AI is not perfect and sometimes it makes mistakes. If the doctor trust the computer too much, the patient can get the wrong treatment. Second, patients' medical information is very private, and if it is stored in computer systems, it can be stolen by hackers. Moreover, many people prefer to talk with a real doctor, because a machine cannot understand their feelings or explain things in a kind way.

In conclusion, I think using artificial intelligence to help doctors is a good idea because it makes the diagnosis quicker and more accurate. The problems like mistakes and privacy are important, but they can be reduced if doctors always check the results of AI. So the advantages outweigh the disadvantages in my opinion.

samples.text:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being introduced into hospitals and clinics to support doctors in diagnosing disease. Although this development raises understandable concerns, I believe that its benefits are greater, as long as the final decision remains in human hands.

Admittedly, relying on AI in medicine involves several risks. No system is completely reliable, and an error in diagnosis could have serious consequences for a patient. There is also a danger that doctors become too dependent to software and gradually lose some of their own diagnostic skills. In addition, these systems need huge amounts of patient data to be trained, which creates concerns about privacy and about who controls such sensitive information. Finally, some patients may feel uneasy if they believe a machine rather than a person is responsible for their care.

Despite these issues, the advantages are more significant. AI tools are able to analyse medical images, such as scans and X-rays, extremely quickly and can often detect subtle patterns that even experienced specialists overlook. This means that serious conditions like cancer or heart disease may be identified at an earlier stage, when treatment is more likely to succeed. Furthermore, AI can reduce the heavy workload of doctors, allowing them to spend more time talking to patients and planning treatment. In regions where specialists are in short supply, a diagnostic tool on a computer or phone could provide an expert first opinion that would otherwise not be available at all.

Most of the disadvantages can also be managed. If AI is used as an assistant rather than a replacement, doctors can check its suggestions, and strict laws on data protection can reduce the risk to privacy.

In conclusion, while artificial intelligence in diagnosis brings risks of error, over-reliance and loss of privacy, its ability to detect illness faster and more accurately makes it a valuable tool. On balance, therefore, the advantages clearly outweigh the drawbacks.
samples.why: Clear position throughout with a definite judgement · ideas extended with relevant examples, though some claims are generalised · logical progression · good range of vocabulary · mostly accurate, one preposition slip.

samples.text:
The use of artificial intelligence to assist in diagnosing illness has moved rapidly from experimental research to everyday clinical practice in many countries. While the technology is not without its hazards, I am convinced that, used responsibly, it offers benefits that far outweigh its drawbacks.

The most compelling case for diagnostic AI lies in its accuracy and consistency. Algorithms trained on vast collections of medical images can identify minute abnormalities in scans that might escape a tired or inexperienced clinician, and unlike humans, they do not become less attentive at the end of a long shift. Earlier detection of conditions such as tumours can transform a patient's prognosis, turning a potentially fatal illness into a treatable one. AI also addresses a practical problem faced by health systems almost everywhere: a shortage of specialists. By screening routine cases, it frees doctors to concentrate on complex diagnoses and on the human side of medicine, and it can extend a degree of specialist expertise to rural clinics that have no radiologist on site.

The concerns, nevertheless, are real. Diagnostic systems are only as good as the data used to build them, so a tool developed mainly with records from one population may perform poorly for others, potentially widening existing inequalities in care. There is also the question of accountability: when an algorithm contributes to a misdiagnosis, it is unclear whether responsibility lies with the doctor, the hospital or the software developer. Moreover, the large-scale collection of health records required to train these systems inevitably raises questions of confidentiality.

Crucially, though, none of these problems is inherent to the technology. They can be mitigated through rigorous testing on diverse patient groups, clear legal frameworks and the principle that AI supports, rather than replaces, clinical judgement.

In conclusion, the risks associated with AI in diagnosis demand careful regulation, but they are outweighed by its potential to detect disease earlier, ease pressure on doctors and bring expert assessment to those who currently lack it.
samples.why: Fully addresses the question with a clear, well-justified judgement · ideas logically sequenced and thoroughly developed · cohesion managed skilfully · wide, precise vocabulary · wide range of structures, error-free.
